newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: More woes seen in store for Singapore retailers.
newsitem.headline: More woes seen in store for Singapore retailers.

text.p: Singapore's battered retailers will continue to suffer from poor demand and tough competition as more and more shops sprout up in a city that would like to become Asia's top shopping centre, analysts say.
Government plans to boost tourism would provide only a glimmer of hope for a retail industry in the doldrums, industry analysts said late last week.
Retailers, plagued by high rents, poor demand, limited tourist growth and heated competition, were unlikely to see a reprieve from a two-year slump any time soon, the analysts said.
Some said they did not expect the sector to see an upturn for at least another year, or maybe two.

"The problem with Singapore's retail sector is there is too much supply coming onstream. There are so many retailers, all chasing a limited number of consumers and competition. It is just too intense," an analyst with stock broker GK Goh Securities said.
The analysts said they were not optimistic that plans by the government to promote Singapore as a tourist hub could lift the retail sector from its trough.
"There could be some spin-off, but it will not be a great one for the retail sector," an analyst from Ong and Co said.

In July, Singapore Minister of Trade and Industry, Yeo Cheow Tong, announced the government's tourist arrival target for the year 2000 was 10 million and forecast a hefty rise in the amount of tourism spending.
The Ong and Co analyst said most people came to Singapore for business rather than pleasure and it was more of an international conference centre than a shopping Mecca.
"These conference attendees are unlikely to be your typical shopaholics," she said.
"At the end of the day, there is only so much Singapore can do. We depend on other factors," an analyst with a local stock brokerage said.
Those factors included keener competition in Asia for the status of tourism hub and global economic strength, she said.
Analysts said it was unlikely the "Great Singapore Sale", a month-long nationwide sale that ended in July, or the various year-end festive bargains would improve profits much.

"It's not a matter of sales. The problem is whether they can maintain or improve margins," the GK Goh analyst said, referring to high operating costs including labour, rents and advertising. In their latest announcements, most retail companies reported dismal results and projected a difficult trading climate.

Underscoring the trend, Robinsons and Company, one of Singapore's oldest homegrown retailers, reported a dip in earnings for the first time in 10 years. It said net profit fell 10.8 percent to S$25.34 million for the year ended June 30.

It said difficult trading conditions coupled with lower consumer spending, higher overheads and intense competition were likely to affect the group's ability to maintain the same level of operating profit as last year.
Some retailers, like Isetan Singapore, managed to return to the black with a S$2.0 million profit after two years of losses. The biggest victim was CK Tang which lost a massive S$28 million.
Retail and property group Metro Holdings saw net profits plunge 84.6 percent to S$1.08 million last year.
